plants.lifeCycle: Biennial or short-lived perennial, usually grown as an annual
plants.hardiness: Perennial in Zones 7-10; grown as an annual elsewhere.

plants.lifeCycle: Tender perennial, usually grown as an annual
plants.hardiness: Perennial in Zones 7-10; grown as an annual in colder climates.
Annual — a cool-season flower; sow in fall in mild climates or early spring elsewhere.

growing.sowing: Direct sow in early spring, or in fall for blooms the next year. Seed sprouts poorly once the soil warms past 55°F, so sow early and cool.
growing.germination: Seed sprouts in 14 to 21 days at about 55°F, sown ¼ inch deep — it needs darkness. Chilling the seed in the fridge for 7 days before sowing improves sprouting.
growing.transplanting: Direct sowing works best. If you start indoors, sow 5 to 7 weeks before planting out, keep the seedlings cool at about 55°F, and move them out while the weather is still cool.
growing.days_to_bloom: About 80 to 90 days from sowing to bloom.
growing.growing: Full sun, in rich, well-drained, slightly alkaline soil. Plants grow 3 to 4 feet tall and do best with support.
growing.harvest_for_cutting: Cut fresh stems when 2 or 3 of the bottom flowers are open, up to about a third of the spike — expect 5 to 7 days in the vase. For dried flowers, cut when the flowers are open but before the petals drop.
good_to_know: Every part of larkspur is poisonous, including the seed — keep it away from children and livestock.

seedSaving.when_to_harvest: Watch the pods as they swell, turn brown, and dry on the stalk. Cut when the seeds rattle inside the pods, but before the pods split and spill.
seedSaving.how_to_collect: Cut whole stalks at the rattle stage and bring them indoors. Dry them about two more weeks, then shake or rub the seed out of the pods into a container.
seedSaving.cleaning: Pour the seed through a sieve and blow off the pod bits. Pick out any pale or shrivelled seed.
seedSaving.drying: Let the stalks finish drying indoors for about two weeks after cutting, then thresh, and give the seed a final airing before storing.
seedSaving.storage: Store in an airtight container in a cool, dark, dry place. Larkspur seed is short-lived — sow it fresh, within a year or two.
seedSaving.pollination_notes: The flowers are open to insects and varieties cross, so grow only one variety if you want pure seed. All parts of larkspur, including the seed, are poisonous — keep saved seed labelled and away from children and livestock.

plants.hardiness: Hardy annual — frost-hardy; fall sowings can come through snow in mild climates.

growing.sowing: Direct sow as soon as the soil can be worked, ¼ inch deep — sow thinly, about 6 seeds to the foot, and keep the surface moist. You can also sow 2 to 4 weeks before the last frost, or in fall in mild climates.
growing.germination: Seed sprouts in 7 to 14 days at 60–65°F. Cover the seed lightly.
growing.transplanting: Direct sowing is best. If you start indoors, sow 3 to 4 weeks before planting out and grow the seedlings cool, with nights around 50–55°F, so they build a good root ball.
growing.days_to_bloom: About 65 to 75 days from sowing to bloom.
growing.spacing: Thin seedlings to 6 to 9 inches apart at the first true leaves.
growing.growing: Full sun. Cornflower tolerates poor soil and is an easy, low-fuss flower that brings in beneficial insects.
growing.harvest_for_cutting: Cut fresh flowers when they are a quarter to half open. The petals are edible.
good_to_know: Cornflower sows itself and naturalises easily — let a few heads ripen if you want it back next year.

seedSaving.when_to_harvest: Let the heads dry on the plant until they are brown, with a furry centre. The ripe seeds are small tan barrels with a little tuft of bristles.
seedSaving.how_to_collect: Cut the dry heads into a paper bag on a dry day. Rub the top of each head between your palms and the seeds roll out.
seedSaving.cleaning: Rub the heads apart, then winnow in front of a low fan, or blow across the seed, to lift off the light chaff.
seedSaving.drying: Bring the heads in and let them cure 1 to 2 weeks, then rub the seed out and give it a couple more days of airing before storing.
seedSaving.storage: Keep in paper envelopes in a cool, dark, dry place. Cornflower seed stays good for a few years.
seedSaving.pollination_notes: Open-pollinated cornflowers come true, but bees cross the colours, so a mixed patch gives mixed colours. Seed from F1 hybrids will not grow true.

plants.hardiness: Hardy annual — frost-hardy.

growing.sowing: Direct sow in spring; it does best sown where it will grow. For a long run of flowers and pods, sow again every 2 to 3 weeks through spring.
growing.germination: Seed sprouts in 10 to 14 days at 60–65°F. Sow about ⅛ inch deep.
growing.transplanting: It can be started indoors 4 to 6 weeks before the last frost, but the taproot is touchy about being moved — handle seedlings gently, or just direct sow.
growing.days_to_bloom: About 65 to 75 days from sowing to bloom.
growing.spacing: Thin or space plants about 8 inches apart.
growing.growing: Full sun. Nigella is easy and undemanding, and it sows itself around the garden.
growing.harvest_for_cutting: Cut fresh stems when the buds are fully coloured, or the pods have just begun to form. For dried use, cut when the seed pods feel firm.
good_to_know: Nigella sows itself readily — let a few pods ripen and drop and it will be back next year.

seedSaving.when_to_harvest: Let the pods dry on the plant until they turn papery and buff-tan and the stripes fade. Shake one — ripe seed rattles inside the crunchy, balloon-like pod.
seedSaving.how_to_collect: Snip the dry pods into a paper bag, or cut the stems and hang them upside down over a sheet. Crush or shake the pods and the black seed falls out through the opening at the top.
seedSaving.cleaning: Pour the seed through a sieve and blow or winnow off the light pod flakes. Spread it out and pick over any green or soft seed.
seedSaving.drying: Spread the seed in a thin layer indoors for about a week, until it is hard and dry.
seedSaving.storage: Store in a paper envelope or sealed jar in a cool, dark, dry place. Expect it to stay good for roughly 2 to 5 years.
seedSaving.pollination_notes: Bees cross the colours freely, so a mixed patch gives mixed colours in the seed you save. Keep one variety about a quarter mile from others for pure seed.

plants.hardiness: Annual — frost-tolerant; it blooms from summer right up to a heavy frost.

growing.sowing: Direct sow after the danger of frost, ¼ inch deep — direct sowing is the standard way. Make 2 or 3 sowings, 2 to 3 weeks apart, for a steady run of flowers.
growing.germination: Seed sprouts in 7 to 14 days at about 70°F.
growing.transplanting: You can also start indoors 4 to 5 weeks before planting out, and move seedlings out around the last frost.
growing.days_to_bloom: About 50 to 55 days from sowing to bloom.
growing.growing: Sun or part shade, in rich, well-drained soil. Calendula is frost-tolerant and keeps blooming late into fall.
growing.harvest_for_cutting: Cut flowers when they are about half open. The petals are edible — pull them from fully open flowers, but don't eat the green base or the centre of the flower.

seedSaving.when_to_harvest: The seeds ripen fast and drop quickly, so check plants often. Pick heads as they turn brown and tan, while the curved, crescent-shaped seeds are still held in the head — or slip a small bag over ripening heads to catch what falls.
seedSaving.how_to_collect: Rub or brush the dry heads over a bowl and the crescent seeds come away easily. Heads picked a touch green will finish ripening as they dry.
seedSaving.cleaning: Shake out loose petal bits and blow off the light chaff. Pick out any soft, green seed.
seedSaving.drying: Spread the seed in a single layer in a dry, airy place for 3 to 7 days, up to a week or two, until a seed snaps rather than bends.
seedSaving.storage: Store in an envelope or jar in a cool, dark, dry place. Calendula seed is best sown within a few years — figure on about 3 years of good life, sometimes longer.
seedSaving.pollination_notes: Calendula mostly pollinates itself and crossing is uncommon, but bees can carry pollen between varieties. Grow one variety, or keep varieties about 700 feet apart, for seed that comes true.

plants.hardiness: Hardy annual — seedlings tolerate light frost.

growing.sowing: Sow indoors 4 to 5 weeks before you plant out, or direct sow early. Sweet peas need about 50 days of cool weather, under 60°F, to bloom well, so get them in early.
growing.germination: Seed sprouts in 14 to 21 days at 55–65°F. Soaking the seed for 24 hours before sowing helps, and it should be sown ¼ to ½ inch deep — it needs darkness to sprout.
growing.transplanting: Plant seedlings out about a month before the last frost — they handle light frost fine. Set them 4 to 8 inches apart along their support.
growing.days_to_bloom: About 75 to 85 days from sowing to first flowers.
growing.growing: Give them a trellis or netting to climb — support is a must. Pinch the growing tip when plants are 6 to 8 inches tall to make them branch.
growing.harvest_for_cutting: Cut in the coolest part of the day, when 2 or 3 flowers on the stem are open, and get the stems straight into water. Expect about 4 to 7 days in the vase. Keep picking — once the plants set seed in the heat, flowering stops.
good_to_know: The seeds and pods are poisonous — don't eat them, and keep them away from livestock.

seedSaving.when_to_harvest: Leave the pods on the vine until they are brown, dry, and plump. Pick them before they pop open and scatter the seed.
seedSaving.how_to_collect: Snip the pods off, leaving a few inches of stem on each. Spread them on a screen, or hang them, in a dry, warm place until they split, then shell the seed out by hand.
seedSaving.cleaning: Shell the peas out and pick over them, tossing any shrivelled or discoloured seed. The seed is big, so there is little chaff to deal with.
seedSaving.drying: Spread the shelled seed in a dry, warm spot and let it dry further, until it is hard, before you store it.
seedSaving.storage: Keep in a sealed jar or envelope in a cool, dark, dry place. Stored well, sweet pea seed stays viable about 3 to 5 years.
seedSaving.pollination_notes: Sweet peas mostly pollinate themselves inside their closed flowers, so varieties usually come true without isolation — but crosses do happen, so saved seed is not guaranteed true.

plants.lifeCycle: Short-lived perennial, often grown as a biennial or annual
plants.hardiness: Perennial in Zones 2-8; often grown as a biennial or annual.
Hardy annual — sown in fall or early spring; self-sows freely.
Hardy annual — sow in spring or fall; self-seeds.
Hardy annual — the foliage shrugs off light frosts.

growing.sowing: Direct sow in early spring, or in late summer and fall for earlier blooms. It makes a fragile taproot and hates being moved, so sow it where it will grow.
growing.germination: Seed sprouts in 14 to 21 days at 60–65°F. Scatter it on the surface and do not cover it — the seed needs light.
growing.transplanting: Do not transplant. Poppies grow a fragile taproot and take transplanting very poorly, so direct sowing is the way.
growing.days_to_bloom: About 80 to 90 days from sowing to bloom.
growing.spacing: Thin seedlings to 8 to 10 inches apart.
growing.growing: Full sun and soil that drains well. Once it is up and growing it asks for little.
good_to_know: Breadseed poppy sows itself freely — leave a few dry pods standing and you will have plants again next year.

seedSaving.when_to_harvest: Wait until the pods have dried on the plant and turned tan. Give a pod a shake — when the seeds rattle inside, they are ripe.
seedSaving.how_to_collect: Cut the dry pods and tip them over a bowl or bucket. The ripe seed pours out through the little holes that open under the crown of the pod, like a pepper shaker.
seedSaving.cleaning: Pour the seed through a fine sieve, or blow gently across it, to lift out bits of pod and dust. Pick out any pale, soft seed.
seedSaving.drying: Spread the seed thin on a tray or screen in a dry, airy spot for a few days, until it is hard and fully dry, before you jar it.
seedSaving.storage: Keep in a sealed jar in a cool, dark, dry place. Poppy seed is short-lived — plan on about 2 years.
seedSaving.pollination_notes: Bees work the flowers and varieties cross readily, so grow only one variety, or keep varieties about 300 feet apart, for seed that comes true.

plants.hardiness: Annual — plant out after frost; the first frost ends it.

growing.sowing: Start indoors 4 weeks before planting out, or direct sow ¼ inch deep once the weather warms. Zinnias grow fast, so don't start them too early.
growing.germination: Seed sprouts fast — 3 to 5 days at 80–85°F, or 5 to 7 days at 70–75°F. Cover the seed lightly; a heat mat helps.
growing.transplanting: Move plants out after the danger of frost. Don't let seedlings sit and get root-bound, and handle the roots gently — rough transplanting can make double varieties throw single flowers.
growing.days_to_bloom: About 75 to 90 days from sowing to bloom.
growing.growing: Full sun and good air movement — space and airflow keep powdery mildew down.
growing.harvest_for_cutting: Cut as soon as the stem has firmed up: hold the stem about 8 inches below the bloom and give it a wiggle — if it flops, wait; if it stands stiff, cut. Zinnias don't open any further in the vase. Cut stems last about 7 to 10 days.

seedSaving.when_to_harvest: Leave the heads on the plant until they are completely dry and brown, and the stem just below the head has browned too. Ripe seed is the stiff, arrowhead-shaped seed at the base of each petal.
seedSaving.how_to_collect: Cut the dry heads and crumble or rub them apart over a tray. The seeds pull free from the dried head.
seedSaving.cleaning: Winnow with a fan or your breath — the light, papery chaff blows away, and takes immature seed and disease-carrying bits with it. Keep only plump, firm seed.
seedSaving.drying: Spread the seed in a thin layer out of direct sun and let it dry at least 3 weeks, stirring it once or twice a day, before storing.
seedSaving.storage: Store airtight in a cool, dark, dry place. Well-kept zinnia seed stays good for about 5 years.
seedSaving.pollination_notes: Zinnias mostly pollinate themselves, and you can bag or cage a few heads to keep them pure. For field seed, grow one variety per season, or keep varieties several hundred feet apart.

plants.hardiness: Annual — sow after the last frost.

growing.sowing: Direct sow after the last frost, ½ inch deep. Sow every 1 to 2 weeks for single-stem types, or every 2 to 3 weeks for branching types, to keep flowers coming.
growing.germination: Seed sprouts in 7 to 14 days at 70–75°F.
growing.transplanting: Direct sowing is best — sunflowers dislike root disturbance. If you start indoors, sow only 2 to 3 weeks before planting out and move them gently.
growing.days_to_bloom: From sowing: about 50 to 65 days for ProCut types, 60 to 70 days for Sunrich types, and 60 to 75 days for branching mixes.
growing.spacing: Spacing sets the bloom size: 4 to 6 inches apart for single-stem cutting flowers, 18 to 24 inches for branching types.
growing.growing: Full sun. Pinch branching varieties to encourage more stems — but never pinch single-stem types, or you will get poor blooms or none.
growing.harvest_for_cutting: Cut when the colour first shows on the petals, or wait until the flower is almost fully open — either stage works for the vase.
good_to_know: Single-stem types make one flower per plant. Many cutting sunflowers are pollenless hybrids — nice for arrangements, but their seed won't grow true.

seedSaving.when_to_harvest: The back of the head turns from green to yellow to brown, the petals drop, and the head hangs heavy and droops. The seeds should be plump, firm, and fully striped.
seedSaving.how_to_collect: Slip a paper bag over ripening heads to keep the birds off. Cut the head with a length of stem and hang it upside down in a dry, airy place for 1 to 2 weeks, then rub the seeds out by hand.
seedSaving.cleaning: Rub the seeds loose and pour them in front of a fan to winnow away the light chaff. Pick out any soft or empty seeds.
seedSaving.drying: Hang cut heads upside down in a dry, airy spot for 1 to 2 weeks, until the seeds rub out easily and feel hard and dry.
seedSaving.storage: Store in a sealed jar or envelope in a cool, dark, dry place. Sunflower seed keeps about 1 to 3 years, losing strength as it ages — sow the freshest first.
seedSaving.pollination_notes: Bees cross sunflowers freely, so keep varieties about half a mile apart for pure seed. Save seed only from open-pollinated or heirloom kinds — hybrid (F1) seed will not grow true.

plants.lifeCycle: Tender perennial, often grown as an annual
plants.hardiness: Perennial in Zones 7-10 where the tubers are mulched; dig and store the tubers where winters are colder.
Annual — plant out after the danger of frost; it wants real warmth.

growing.sowing: Start indoors 6 to 8 weeks before planting out. Direct sowing only works where the season is long — sow ⅛ inch deep after the last frost.
growing.germination: Seed sprouts in 8 to 14 days at 70–80°F. The seed needs light, so cover it only very lightly. Water from below, or mist, so the tiny seed isn't washed away.
growing.transplanting: Grow seedlings warm, at about 63–68°F, harden them off, and move them out only after the danger of frost has passed. Cold weather and short days can make young plants flower too early, so don't rush them out.
growing.days_to_bloom: Plume types take about 85 to 100 days from sowing. Cockscomb types vary widely by variety, roughly 55 to 120 days.
growing.growing: Full sun and well-drained, moist, fertile soil. Pinch the growing tip at 6 to 12 inches tall on plume and crested types grown for many stems — but don't pinch the single-flower production types, which make one flower per plant.
growing.harvest_for_cutting: Cut fresh when the flowers are fully developed and the stem feels firm at the base of the bloom — they last 7 to 14 days in the vase. For drying, cut at the same stage, strip the leaves, and hang the stems in a dark, airy place.
good_to_know: Celosia sows itself in the garden — expect volunteers where heads ripened last year.

seedSaving.when_to_harvest: Wait until the seeds inside the heads have dried and start to drop on their own. The tiny, glossy black seeds collect at the base of the papery flower heads.
seedSaving.how_to_collect: Cut the whole heads and hang them to dry a little further, then shake and rub them over a bowl or screen so the little black seeds fall free of the papery husks.
seedSaving.cleaning: Shake the seed out and winnow or sieve away the papery husks and dust. The seed is tiny, so work over a tray or cloth to catch it.
seedSaving.drying: Hang the cut heads in a dry, airy place until they are fully crisp, then thresh the seed out and give it a final airing before storing.
seedSaving.storage: Store in a sealed jar or envelope in a cool, dark, dry place. Celosia seed keeps about 4 years in good storage.
seedSaving.pollination_notes: Celosia pollinates itself, but insects cross varieties too, so keep varieties about a quarter mile apart for pure seed.

plants.hardiness: Annual — plant out after frost.

growing.sowing: Start indoors 5 to 7 weeks before planting out, or direct sow after the last frost once the soil is above 60°F.
growing.germination: Seed sprouts in 7 to 10 days at 68–72°F. Cover the seed lightly.
growing.transplanting: Harden seedlings off and move them out after the danger of frost, spacing them 9 to 12 inches apart.
growing.days_to_bloom: Cosmos bipinnatus takes about 90 to 110 days from sowing. Cosmos sulphureus is faster, at about 65 to 75 days.
growing.spacing: Space plants 9 to 12 inches apart — wider spacing gives stronger, thicker stems.
growing.growing: Full sun. Pinch young plants to make them branch, keep cutting or deadheading for flowers all summer, and give tall varieties some netting or support to lean on.
growing.harvest_for_cutting: Cut when the petals are just opening, before the flower flattens out.

seedSaving.when_to_harvest: The seed ripens fast and shatters, so watch the heads closely and pick each one as it ripens. Ripe seeds are the slender, dark, double-pointed sticks in the centre of the spent head — a ripe one flicks loose easily.
seedSaving.how_to_collect: On a dry day, snip the ripening heads straight into a bag so nothing drops. Rub the heads over a screen to free the seed.
seedSaving.cleaning: Rub the heads apart and pick out the firm, dark seeds, discarding soft or green ones. Blow off the light chaff.
seedSaving.drying: Spread the seed in a single layer in a dry place. It can take several weeks to dry all the way through — be patient before storing.
seedSaving.storage: Keep in a sealed jar or envelope in a cool, dark, dry place. Cosmos seed stays viable about 5 years in good storage.
seedSaving.pollination_notes: Bees cross cosmos, so keep varieties about a quarter mile apart for pure seed. The two garden species, Cosmos bipinnatus and Cosmos sulphureus, usually don't cross with each other.

plants.hardiness: Annual — grown in a single season.

plants.lifeCycle: Biennial to short-lived perennial, usually grown as an annual
plants.hardiness: Perennial in Zones 3-7; usually grown as an annual.
Annual — plant out after the danger of frost has passed.

growing.sowing: Start indoors 4 to 6 weeks before planting out. Where summers are long, you can direct sow instead.
growing.germination: Seed sprouts in 7 to 10 days at 70–75°F. Do not cover the seed — it needs light. Water from below, or mist gently, so the tiny seeds don't wash away.
growing.transplanting: Harden seedlings off and move them out after the danger of frost has passed, spacing them 10 to 12 inches apart.
growing.days_to_bloom: About 75 to 85 days from sowing to bloom.
growing.growing: Full sun and average soil with good drainage. Pinch young plants to make them branch, and tall plants may need support. Plants grow about 3 feet tall.
growing.harvest_for_cutting: Cut when 2 or 3 layers of petals have opened, but before the flower opens all the way and shows its centre — pick on a bright morning. Over-ripe blooms fall apart when dried.
good_to_know: Strawflower is an excellent dried flower — cut extra stems for winter arrangements.

seedSaving.when_to_harvest: Leave some heads on the plant well past their pretty stage, until the papery bracts are fully dry and the centre of the head turns fluffy, like a tiny dandelion clock.
seedSaving.how_to_collect: Cut the fully dry heads and rub them between your hands over a bowl. The ripe seed shakes loose from the fluffy centre.
seedSaving.cleaning: Rub the heads to release the seed, then blow or winnow off the fluff and chaff. Pick out any soft seed.
seedSaving.drying: Air-dry the heads 7 to 10 days in a dry spot, before or after rubbing the seed out, until everything is crisp and dry.
seedSaving.storage: Keep in a sealed jar or envelope in a cool, dark, dry place. Strawflower seed is fairly short-lived — plan on about 2 years.
seedSaving.pollination_notes: Strawflowers mostly pollinate themselves, but insects can carry pollen between varieties. Open-pollinated varieties come true as long as they don't share pollen with another variety nearby.

Annual — grown in a single season.

Annual — grown in a single season.
Hardy annual — frost-tolerant to about 19°F; fall-sown in Zones 5 and up.
Annual — grown in a single season; only in frost-free Zones 10-11 does it persist as a short-lived perennial.
Hardy annual — tolerates light frost; fall-planted and overwintered in warmer zones.

plants.lifeCycle: Short-lived perennial, usually grown as an annual
plants.hardiness: Perennial in Zones 8-10; grown as an annual elsewhere; self-seeds freely.
Hardy annual — sown in spring or fall; self-seeds.
Hardy in Zones 4-8 — sow in early summer and overwinter the rosette for second-year blooms.

plants.lifeCycle: Tender perennial, usually grown as an annual
plants.hardiness: Perennial in Zones 6-8; usually grown as an annual.
Annual — plant after the last frost; killed by frost.

plants.lifeCycle: Biennial, most often grown as an annual
plants.hardiness: Grown as an annual in cold climates; behaves as a biennial in Zones 7 and warmer.
Annual — a cool-season flower; sow in fall or early spring.
Annual — sow in fall in mild climates (Zones 8-10) or early spring; self-seeds.
Annual — a cool-season flower; sow in fall or early spring.
Hardy annual — very cold-tolerant; sow in spring or fall.
Annual — a fast cool-season crop; tolerates light frost but bolts in heat.

plants.lifeCycle: Tender perennial, grown as an annual
plants.hardiness: Perennial in Zones 9-11; grown as an annual in colder climates.
Annual — grown in a single season in Zones 2-11; self-seeds freely.

plants.hardiness: Perennial in Zones 8-10; grown as an annual in colder climates.

plants.lifeCycle: Annual or short-lived perennial, usually grown as an annual
plants.hardiness: Short-lived perennial in Zones 7-10; grown as an annual elsewhere; self-seeds freely.

plants.lifeCycle: Tender perennial, grown as an annual
plants.hardiness: Perennial in Zones 10-11; grown as an annual in colder climates.

plants.lifeCycle: Tender perennial, grown as an annual
plants.hardiness: Perennial in Zones 8-11; grown as an annual elsewhere; reseeds readily.
Hardy annual — grown in Zones 2-11; self-sows freely.
Hardy annual — tolerates light frost; self-seeds.
Annual — not frost-hardy; sow in spring after frost danger.

plants.lifeCycle: Tender perennial, grown as an annual
plants.hardiness: Perennial in Zones 9-11; grown as an annual in colder climates.
Perennial in Zones 4-8 — short-lived, especially where summers are hot and humid; let it self-sow.
Hardy annual — direct sow a few weeks before the last frost.
Annual — plant out after the danger of frost.

growing.sowing: Start indoors 4 to 6 weeks before planting out — or 8 weeks ahead if you want them already in flower. Direct sowing ¼ inch deep works too.
growing.germination: Seed sprouts in 4 to 7 days at 75–80°F. Cover the seed lightly.
growing.transplanting: Move seedlings out after the danger of frost has passed.
growing.days_to_bloom: From sowing: about 50 days for French types, 60 days for signet (Gem) types, and 70 to 90 days for African types.
growing.spacing: Space French types 8 to 12 inches apart, Gem types about 12 inches, and African types 12 to 18 inches.
growing.growing: Full sun. Marigolds are easy, steady bloomers from summer until frost.
growing.harvest_for_cutting: Cut when the flowers are fully open but the centres are still tight.

seedSaving.when_to_harvest: Let the heads dry completely on the plant, until they are brown, papery, and shrivelled. Inside each dried cup sits a bundle of ripe seed.
seedSaving.how_to_collect: Pull the dry heads and squeeze or pull them apart over a bowl. The seeds — slim black sticks with a pale tip, like tiny paintbrushes — fall right out.
seedSaving.cleaning: Pull the seed bundles apart and shake out loose bits of petal and cup. There is little chaff; just pick out any soft or green seed.
seedSaving.drying: Spread the seed out for a few days, up to 1 to 2 weeks, until it is fully dry before storing.
seedSaving.storage: Keep in an envelope or jar in a cool, dark, dry place. Marigold seed stays viable about 5 years in good storage.
seedSaving.pollination_notes: Marigolds pollinate themselves, but bees can cross varieties, so keep varieties about a quarter mile apart for pure seed. Seed saved from hybrids will not grow true to the parent plant.

growing.sowing: Start indoors 4 to 6 weeks before the last frost, or direct sow about 2 weeks before the last frost. Make another planting every 2 to 3 weeks until midsummer for a steady run of flowers.
growing.germination: Seed sprouts in 10 to 12 days at 65–70°F. Sow on the surface — the seed needs light to sprout.
growing.transplanting: Move seedlings out after the danger of frost has passed, spacing them 8 to 12 inches apart.
growing.days_to_bloom: About 90 to 100 days from sowing to first flowers.
growing.growing: Full sun. Tall plants may need support to keep the stems straight for cutting.
growing.harvest_for_cutting: Cut when the flowers are almost fully open — about three-quarters open is the sweet spot. The green seed heads are good in arrangements too. Cut flowers last about 7 to 10 days in the vase.

seedSaving.when_to_harvest: Leave the heads on the plant until they are fully dry and brown or tan. Start picking as soon as the first seeds begin to loosen and shatter — wait too long and the rest drops.
seedSaving.how_to_collect: Cut the dry heads straight into a paper bag so you don't lose seed on the way. Rub or crush the heads between your hands to free the seed from its little compartments.
seedSaving.cleaning: Rub the heads over a screen, then winnow by pouring the seed in front of a gentle fan, or blowing across it, to carry off the chaff.
seedSaving.drying: Spread the cleaned seed thin in a dry, airy place until it is fully dry and hard before storing.
seedSaving.storage: Keep in a sealed jar or envelope in a cool, dark, dry place. In good storage it stays viable up to about 3 years.
seedSaving.pollination_notes: Insects cross scabiosa readily, so grow one variety at a time, or isolate varieties, to keep seed true. Seed from hybrid varieties will not grow true to the parent.

growing.sowing: Start indoors in late winter, or sow outside in fall and let winter do the chilling for you. A stretch of cold, damp conditions in the fridge — 8 to 12 weeks — improves sprouting for spring sowing.
growing.germination: Seed sprouts in 10 to 21 days at about 65–72°F. Sow ⅛ to ¼ inch deep.
growing.transplanting: Start indoors 8 to 10 weeks before you want to plant out. Move plants outside after frost, once the soil has warmed.
growing.days_to_bloom: Expect flowers in the second year — echinacea spends its first year building a strong root and crown.
growing.growing: Full sun, at least 6 hours a day, and soil that drains well. Once settled in, it handles drought well, and it sows itself freely.
good_to_know: Leave the standing seed heads for the goldfinches — they love them — and expect seedlings to pop up around the parent plants.

seedSaving.when_to_harvest: Let the cones dry on the plant until they are dark brown to black, crisp, and prickly. Rub a cone with a gloved thumb — ripe seed loosens and starts to come away.
seedSaving.how_to_collect: Cut the dry cones into a paper bag before they shatter and drop their seed. Rub the cones hard between your palms, or shake the heads in a lidded can, to knock the seed free.
seedSaving.cleaning: The seed is heavier than the chaff, so blow across it, or pour it in front of a fan, and the light bits lift away. Pick out any soft or pale seed.
seedSaving.drying: If the cones feel at all damp, spread or hang them in a dry, airy place for 2 to 3 weeks to finish drying before you rub the seed out.
seedSaving.storage: Store in a sealed jar in a cool, dark, dry place. In good storage it stays viable about 2 to 3 years.
seedSaving.pollination_notes: The common garden species are open-pollinated and come true when grown on their own, but the species cross with each other and hybrids pop up — grow one kind by itself for true seed.

varieties.description: Tall, strongly fragrant cut flower stock with 32" stems and very early, programmable timing (7–11 weeks in fall, 8–13 weeks in spring). Uniform stem length across the mix. Approximately 50% double flowering, which is normal for stock. Best suited for cool greenhouse, tunnel, or open field.
varieties.sowingNotes: Sow November in pots or trays under cool cover (45–55°F). Can also be sown January–February as an insurance sowing using the same seed. Grows best in cool, bright conditions — cold frame or unheated greenhouse, not a warm house.

varieties.description: Classic 30" cut flower snapdragon, fragrant, with strong upright spikes suited for field or greenhouse production. The Rocket series is a standard professional cut flower choice. Available in individual colours (Bronze, Golden Yellow, Orchid, Pink, Red, White) and mix.
varieties.sowingNotes: Sow November in pots or trays under cool cover (45–55°F). Also sow January–February for a second wave. Needs cool, bright conditions to develop strong stems.

varieties.description: Tall double azalea-flowered snapdragon, 30", described as a superb cut flower. F1 hybrid for uniform timing and stem quality. AAS award winner. Available in individual colours (Bronze, Ivory, Pink, Red, Yellow) and mix.
varieties.sowingNotes: Sow November in pots or trays under cool cover (45–55°F). Also suitable for a January–February insurance sowing.

varieties.description: Group IV tall snapdragon (32–40") with solid spikes on sturdy stems. Named replacement for the discontinued Costa Summer series. Well suited to greenhouse, tunnel, or open ground production.
varieties.sowingNotes: Sow November in pots or trays under cool cover (45–55°F). Also suitable for January–February insurance sowing.

varieties.description: Giant Imperial type larkspur at 32", a reliable direct-sown cut flower. The Imperial Choice Mix is an exact match for traditional cut flower larkspur plantings. Direct sow only — taproot resents transplanting. Suited to the back of the border.
varieties.sowingNotes: Direct sow outdoors in November into a raised, well-drained bed. Cold stratification happens naturally over winter. Most fall sowing failures are caused by poor drainage, not cold. Do not transplant.

varieties.description: Extra-select double bicolour cornflower mix suited to field-grown cut flower, borders, and mass landscape plantings. Direct sown. The Frosty Mix includes frosted bicolour tones not found in standard bachelor's button mixes.
varieties.sowingNotes: Direct sow outdoors in November into a raised, well-drained bed. Hardy annual that benefits from cold conditioning over winter.

varieties.description: Traditional double-flowered Love-in-a-Mist, direct sown to field. Both the intricate blue-green flowers and the striped, inflated seed pods are useful in arrangements. Available in single colours (Indigo, Light Blue, White) and mix.
varieties.sowingNotes: Direct sow outdoors in November. Taproot — does not transplant well. Scatter seed in a prepared bed.

varieties.description: 24" long-stemmed calendula with double and semi-double flowers in orange, apricot, cream, and lemon tones. A classic direct-sown cut flower. Available in single colours (Apricot, Cream, Lemon, Orange w/ Brown Eye) and mix.
varieties.sowingNotes: Direct sow outdoors in November into a well-drained bed. Can also be sown in early spring. Cold-hardy and tolerant of light frost.

varieties.description: 6-foot fragrant climbing sweet pea bred specifically for cut flower production under short days — the best fit for a November sowing aimed at late April to May flowering. Available in single colours (Burgundy, Deep Rose, Mid Blue, White) and mix. Note: a Bed 3 fence row will require multiple packs as each pack is only 100 seeds.
varieties.sowingNotes: Sow November in deep root-trainers under cool cover (45–55°F). Pre-chill seed 4 weeks at 32–35°F, then soak overnight before sowing 1" deep. Needs a trellis or fence. Quantity note: 100 seeds per Trade Pkt — plan on multiple packs for a full fence row.

varieties.description: Sweet pea mix; approximately 300 seeds per ounce. A practical choice for large-scale plantings where a named Spencer variety is not required.
varieties.sowingNotes: Sow in deep root-trainers under cool cover. Pre-soak overnight. Needs a trellis or fence. Climbs to 6 feet.

varieties.description: F1 hybrid Iceland poppy, 15", with uniform timing, sturdy stems, and large flowers. Primed seed for reliable germination. Available in single colours (Orange, Pink, Scarlet, White, Yellow) and mix.
varieties.sowingNotes: Sow November in individual pots — Iceland poppies strongly resent root disturbance. Keep cool and bright (cold frame or unheated greenhouse). Do not transplant bareroot.

varieties.description: 2-foot double Shirley-type poppy mix in cherry, cream, orange, lilac, and mauve bicolour tones. A fresh local cut flower classic, field sown. The American Legion (red Flanders type) is a separate variety — Angel's Choir is the Shirley mix.
varieties.sowingNotes: Direct sow outdoors in November into a well-drained bed. Scatter seed on the surface; poppies need light to germinate. Do not bury seed deeply.

varieties.description: Low-growing front-of-border filler with fragrant small flowers.
varieties.sowingNotes: Direct sow. Suited to front-of-border or low edging. Can be scattered in gaps between taller plants.

varieties.description: Classic ornamental and culinary poppy with large, showy flowers and ornamental seedpods useful in dried arrangements.
varieties.sowingNotes: Direct sow late fall for natural cold stratification. 1,266,000 seeds per pound. Scatter on the soil surface; needs light to germinate.
